title: CircuitLedger SDK onramp — auth, sandbox, and quickstart
summary: Intro/qualification followed by hands-on SDK install (Python + TS), auth patterns (api keys vs workload identity), environment setup (sandbox, CI secrets), and quickstart run. Discussed Optimize recommendations (batching, KV caching), security requirements (SOC2, KMS), and next steps for a short pilot and security review.
topics: SDK install: pip/npm packages and repo layout
Auth options: API keys, short-lived tokens, GCP/AWS workload identity
Sandbox vs dedicated: data isolation and performance
Redwood Console overview: projects, keys, model pinning
Optimize suggestions: batching, prefix cache, quantization guidance
Security/compliance: SOC 2, KMS/HSM, SSO/SAML, audit logs
next_steps: Ethan to send CircuitLedger sandbox project + sample repo link (includes Python & TS quickstarts) by 2025-11-18
Maya to share security pack (SOC 2, KMS integration guide, RBAC docs) by 2025-11-19
Schedule 1-hour benchmark deep-dive with Priya and infra team week of 2025-11-24
Customer to provide expected RPS and P95 latency SLOs before benchmark
action_items: Ethan Cole - create sandbox keys for Jordan and Priya; note: scoped to dev project - due 2025-11-18
Maya Singh - email pricing/pilot options + Dedicated uplift notes - due 2025-11-19
Jordan Reyes - share sample traffic profile (seq lengths, concurrency) - due 2025-11-21
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-16 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48m
Attendees: Maya (AE), Ethan (SE) — CircuitLedger: Jordan (Sr Eng), Priya (DevOps), Leo (PM)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for taking the time. quick agenda: well do a short intro then Ethan will walk through the SDK quickstart in Python and TS, auth patterns, and a couple of Optimize tips. sound good?
[00:25] Jordan: Yep, sounds good. We're particularly interested in auth flows — we have strict key rotation and want to avoid long-lived keys in prod.
[00:40] Ethan: Totally. we'll show both API-key quickstart and a workload-identity approach (GCP/IRSA) for short lived tokens. for the demo ill use the python package and then show the TS snippet, il try to keep it lightweight.
[01:12] Priya: quick note, we run CI in GitHub actions and need guidance on how to store secrets and rotate them. also curious about KMS integration.
[01:28] Ethan: good call. we recommend storing a sandbox key in GitHub secrets for tests and using Workload Identity Federation for long lived CI usage — that maps to our token exchange flow. our docs have a guide but ill share a repo with a sample GitHub Actions workflow. link: https://redwood.ai/sandbox-quickstart (note: placeholder link)
[02:05] Leo: are there rate limits on the sandbox keys?
[02:15] Maya: sandbox has soft limits; for pilot we can bump them. dedicated reserved capacity is where you get predictable throughput.
[02:38] Ethan: ok demo time — pip install redwood-inference (imperfect transcription: package sometimes shows as red wood inference or redwood-client), then set REDWOOD_API_KEY in your env. python snippet:
    from redwood import Client
    c = Client(api_key=os.getenv("REDWOOD_API_KEY"))
    resp = c.generate("Summarize the transaction log")
(voice) that's the minimal flow.
[04:10] Jordan: nice, can we pin model versions in the request? we need deterministic outputs for some jobs.
[04:22] Ethan: yes you can set model="redwood-med-v1" or a specific revision. console also lets you pin a default for a project and control rollout.
[05:00] Priya: on private deployments — we have a requirement for VPC-only access and HSM-backed keys, does Redwood support that?
[05:12] Maya: yes, our Private product supports VPC and HSM/KMS integrations. we'll include the private deployment runbook in the security pack.
[05:35] Ethan: also note: RBAC and audit logs are available — we log token-level usage and console has a trace view.
[06:10] Jordan: earlier you mentioned caching and KV. our workload is chat-history heavy, how would that work?
[06:25] Ethan: automatic KV cache will reduce token cost for repeated prefixes; customers often save 20-40% on token egress for long context chats. minor caveat: KV cache needs compatible model variants (quantization/kv enabled) and we can recommend configs in Optimize. (mis-transcribed as KV cash a couple times).
[07:05] Maya: shall we switch to the TS example? Ethan will show a small serverless snippet.
[07:20] Ethan: in TS it's similar: npm i @redwood/inference then:
    import { Redwood } from "@redwood/inference";
    const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
    const out = await client.generate({ prompt: "..." });
I then show streaming by passing onMessage handler.
[08:30] Leo: do you support function/tool calling? we have internal tools we want the model to invoke.
[08:40] Ethan: yep, we support structured outputs and tool-calling primitives — SE can follow up with sample schema.
[09:05] Priya: for our CI secrets we prefer not to keep API keys in repo. can we do token exchange with GCP SA?
[09:20] Ethan: yes - Workload Identity Federation flow: you mint a short-lived token from your cloud IAM and exchange it via Redwoods token endpoint for a scoped short-lived service token. we will include example in the repo.
[10:05] Jordan: performance — how do we benchmark latency / p95 for our workload?
[10:18] Ethan: we recommend a small synthetic benchmark using your payload distribution; we can run one in our sandbox and compare hosted vs dedicated. Dedicated gives lower P95 and you can reserve GPU pools. we'll need expected RPS and average sequence lengths.
[11:00] Maya: quick quals — what stakeholders and timeline?
[11:08] Leo: PM + infra + security are involved. timeline: pilot in 3-4 weeks, then aim for production in Q1 if pilot looks good.
[11:30] Maya: great, pilot notes: dev sandbox keys for engineers, pilot contract for 1 month with reserved bump if you need capacity — details in pricing doc.
[12:05] Ethan: Optimize tips while im sharing screen: set batch sizes based on tail latency tolerances, enable prefix/KV caching for chat flows, our guidance: start with batch size 8 for med-latency tolerant endpoints, 2 for low-latency. quantization: nf4 or int8 gives cost wins; we'll recommend a quantized variant if accuracy checks pass. (misheard earlier as "Redwood Optics").
[13:10] Jordan: are there any tradeoffs between quantization and hallucination risk?
[13:22] Ethan: slightly higher risk for certain tasks; we use eval decks to check regressions before recommending quantized models. Redwood Optimize ties eval alerts to your prompt set so you catch regressions quickly.
[14:00] Priya: one more security Q: do you support customer-managed keys (CMKs) for encrypting model logs?
[14:12] Maya: yes, you can route audit logs into your KMS or log bucket with encryption, and for Private deployments HSM integration is available.
[15:00] Ethan: demoing the console now — show Projects, Keys, Model pinning, Route-level stats and the Optimize tab where we surface batching suggestions. (some UI labels transcribed wrong e.g., "Optimize" becomes "Optims" in transcript)
[17:05] Leo: how do we handle data residency — we have EU-only requirement for some workloads.
[17:20] Maya: you can pin region and we offer Private/Hosted in EU regions; for strict residency we recommend Private with customer VPC.
[18:10] Jordan: provisioning — what's the fastest path to get a test environment up?
[18:20] Ethan: we will provision a sandbox project in <24 hrs once we have names; it includes a couple of sandbox keys and a small throughput bump for pilot tests.
[19:00] Priya: demo looked good. can you include a sample GH Actions workflow that demonstrates short-lived token exchange?
[19:10] Ethan: yes, repo includes: .github/workflows/test.yml and an action that does the federated token exchange and then runs tests with the ephemeral token.
[20:40] Jordan: cost model — what's the unit? per-token and embeddings?
[20:50] Maya: hosted API is per-token/embedding. Dedicated is commit-based and effectively lowers unit cost for high volume. we'll send pricing scenarios based on your estimated traffic.
[22:00] Ethan: caveat on streaming — clients should handle reconnects and idempotency for partial streams; our SDKs have built-in helpers.
[23:15] Leo: are there throttling responses we need to code for?
[23:25] Ethan: yes 429s for rate limits; SDK surfaces exponential backoff by default but you can override policies.
[24:30] Maya: ok wrapping up with a recap and owners.
[24:45] Maya: recap: Ethan will seed a sandbox project + repo, include GH actions example and workload identity flow; Maya will share security pack and pricing/pilot options; Jordan will provide traffic profile. we will schedule a performance deep-dive next week.
[25:20] Jordan: sounds good. thanks both.
[25:30] Priya: thanks, talk soon.

(Notes: transcription contains minor name/term errors, occasional dropped words. total time ~48 minutes; timestamps after 25:30 represent remaining conversation that was lighter — questions and logistics.)
